calls.reason: The only evidence is a 2026 review saying long-horizon outcomes are rarely studied. No project histories with a denominator show how often promising vibe-coding projects end badly.
Barclays data shows Lovable traffic fell about 40%, but Replit's revenue rose sharply and Lovable reports strong retention. No churn-reason data links any pullback to reliability limits.

Vendor OX Security reports maintainability anti-patterns in AI code. But the controlled Borg et al. experiment found no maintainability penalty, so the evidence is mixed and none of it isolates amateur vibe coding.

Interview accounts of knowledge-cutoff problems fit the mechanism. The GitChameleon benchmark shows failures even on versions likely seen in training, and nothing isolates training distribution as the cause.
A 'never' forecast with no deadline. Lemkin's SaaStr account and Lovable's security caveats fit the claim, and the CEO's one undocumented success story doesn't refute it.

ResearchCodeBench shows lower scores on tasks newer than training cutoffs, but that is mixed up with task difficulty. The ParShift study shows success on unfamiliar APIs, and neither tests full amateur builds.
